definition: Mountainous means having many mountains, or relating to high, rugged terrain.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word mountainous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know mountainous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Three quarters of the country is mountainous, and only the coastal strip is flat enough to farm.
Hilly ground rises and falls but never reaches true peaks, while mountainous country does.
Alpine is narrower than mountainous, pointing at the high, treeless zone near the summits rather than at the whole mountain landscape.

Rugged means rough, steep, and hard to cross -- a word about texture and difficulty, not height, so a rugged coastline can lie at sea level. Mountainous is the height claim: country that rises into true mountains, whether the going is rough or gentle.

Craggy describes rock that is steep, broken, and jagged, and a craggy headland can stand at the edge of the sea. Mountainous speaks to the scale of whole country -- land built up into real mountains -- rather than to the texture of its rock.

Mountainous means having many mountains, or relating to high, rugged terrain.
A rail company costs two routes of equal length between the same two cities.
The northern route crosses flat farmland and needs nine bridges, no tunnels, and a maximum gradient of one percent.
The southern route climbs three passes above 2,000 metres, requires fourteen tunnels and thirty-one viaducts, and closes for snow most winters.
The engineers price the southern line at four times the northern one, because the country it crosses is mountainous.
Three passes above 2,000 metres, fourteen tunnels, and regular winter closures describe country built of high peaks rather than gentle ground, which is what mountainous means.
Mountainous describes the land itself and, by extension, anything of mountain size, as in a mountainous pile of laundry.
It names one kind of terrain rather than the general subject of terrain, since the arrangement of a region's surface features as a whole is its topography, taught elsewhere in this unit.

The engineers who surveyed the new road between the two provincial capitals reported that a direct route was impossible.
The land between is relentlessly mountainous: ridge after ridge above four thousand metres, with glaciers filling the high valleys.
The road they finally built swings two hundred kilometres out of its way to follow a single river gorge through the ranges.
Even so, it crosses three passes, and each winter the highest of them closes under six metres of snow.
Flat ground is so scarce along the way that the only petrol station for a day's drive stands on land blasted level from the slope.
